messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bus Driver
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 76

The assault happened six years ago, on a Tuesday night after his shift ended. He had stayed late to finish paperwork, and by the time he left the depot the parking lot was nearly empty. A man he’d never seen before asked for directions, then forced him into the back of his own car. He remembers the gravel digging into his knees, the smell of stale coffee and gasoline, and the way the man’s voice was almost gentle when he said, “Don’t make this harder.” He didn’t fight. He still can’t decide if that was smart or weak. For weeks he told no one; he went to work, drove his route, came home, sat in the dark living room. He told his wife he had a stomach bug.

Now, every morning he pulls the bus out of the depot at 5:47 a.m. The headlights cut through the fog along River Road, and for the first fifteen minutes he can almost pretend the world is normal. Then the first passenger boards, a man in a blue jacket about the same height, and his stomach knots. He scans each face that climbs aboard—looks at hands, looks at eyes, looks for the closed-off calm he remembers. He keeps his own hands locked on the wheel at ten and two, even though it makes his shoulders ache by midday. If a passenger stands too close behind his seat, he brakes harder than necessary to make them step back. He never calls out the stops anymore; he just opens the doors and waits.

The route passes a self-storage lot he didn’t used to notice. Now he takes the long way around, adding twelve minutes, because the sight of those roll-up doors brings a cold wash of sweat and the image of the man’s belt buckle against his cheek. His supervisor pulled him aside last week and said, “You’re three minutes late on every circuit, Dave. What’s going on?” He said the traffic was bad. He said he’d do better.

At home, his wife has learned not to touch him from behind. She used to hug him when he walked in the door; now she waits for him to speak first. They sleep in the same bed but he lies on the farthest edge, facing the door. Last month she said, “You’re not here anymore. You’re somewhere I can’t reach.” He wanted to tell her about the parking lot, about the gravel, about how sometimes when he closes his eyes he feels that man’s hand on his neck, but the words get stuck behind his teeth. He got up and went to the garage instead.

He hasn’t driven his personal car in two years. He takes the bus to the depot, then drives the city bus—because in the city bus he has a radio, a camera feed, a door he can open from his seat. In a car he feels trapped. When his daughter asked why he never visits her new apartment, he said the bus route didn’t go that way. She stopped asking.

The worst part is the shame. Not about what happened—about how he reacted. He was bigger than that man. He could have fought. He could have screamed. Instead he did what he was told, and he hates himself for it. He replays it every night in the three hours between lying down and finally sleeping: the decisions he should have made, the way he could have kicked, the moment he didn’t. The self-loathing is a physical weight, a stone in his chest that makes his breath shallow. Some mornings he has to sit in the driver’s seat for five extra minutes before he can turn the key.

He is still driving. He still gets up before dawn. He still opens the door for every passenger, checks every face, avoids every storage lot, brakes too hard, says nothing. He is a bus driver. He is a husband. He is a father who no longer visits his daughter. He is fifty-three years old, and the Tuesday night hasn’t ended yet.
